findings.claim_defeated: 'primitive-mispaired and governed-vocabulary-closed cover the two rules a fourth witness changed, so that what the repository certifies through scripts/verify.py includes them' (scripts/sovrecurrence/fixture.py); 'Two fixture variants close the gap a witness named ... Both now run under scripts/verify.py, which runs selfcheck and not the unit tests' (commit f43ee9a).
findings.observed: Only one of the two rules is certified. Regression R1 reinstates the exact P4-N1 defect - _structural_names collects title and name again - and python scripts/sov_recurrence.py selfcheck exits 0 with all nine variants still reporting their declared defects. Only the unit test test_a_term_in_a_title_is_not_a_declaration fails, and scripts/verify.py runs selfcheck, not the unit tests. The cause is in _stub: every fixture contract is written with "title": f"Fixture {term} declaration", so the mispaired stub written at the custody path carries the title 'Fixture unrelated declaration'. A reader that reads titles finds 'unrelated' there, not 'custody', and refuses the pairing anyway. primitive-mispaired therefore discriminates a wrong-identity contract from a right one, which is a real property, but it cannot discriminate a prose-reading rule from a structure-reading one, which is the property the commit was written for. Regression R2 shows the contrast: demoting governed closures to reported turns selfcheck red by name.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the defect class the witness procedure names first - a check that cannot see what it grades. The branch's own history is four revisions of a shipped description outrunning what the code measures, and pass 4 named that pattern as the reason it refused e898d06. The repair for it is the one repair the repository's gate cannot certify, and a sentence in the fixture says the gate can. A later participant who edits neutrality.py and runs verify will be told the change is safe.
findings.how_derived: Patched scripts/sovrecurrence/neutrality.py in a throwaway copy to add `elif key in ("title", "name") and isinstance(value, str): names.add(value)` before the existing exclusion branch. Confirmed the patch took effect by printing _structural_names for contracts/work-circuit.json, which went from 1 name to 2 including the title sentence. Then ran selfcheck (exit 0) and the unit tests (1 failure).
findings.repair_shape_if_wanted: Not mine to build and not filed elsewhere: it belongs inside this concern. One line of _stub would do it - give the mispaired stub a title carrying the term it is paired with while its $id carries a different one - which is the case a title-reading reader gets wrong and a structure-reading reader gets right.

findings.observed: The declaration rule is a denylist of five prose keys plus a broad identity rule, not an allowlist of schema keywords. It resists every plant in the class the task names, and three edits that declare nothing still take the reading from 9 resolved to 10. B1: adding a root key editorial_id with the value 'discovery guidance for readers' to contracts/node-interface.schema.json, because _identity_names accepts any root key ending _id or _schema whatever it is called. B2: the same with doc_schema. B3: adding a key not on the denylist - rationale - holding a properties dict, because walk descends into every unlisted key and harvests properties keys wherever it finds them. B4: adding examples holding a properties dict, so property names taken from an example instance count as declarations. B4 contradicts a rationale the module states twice: _identity_names' docstring says 'an identifier nested in example data belongs to the example', and test_an_identifier_in_example_data_is_not_the_contract_identity pins that for identity, while the declared-names half does the opposite. B5 and B6 confirm the denylist and the root-only identity rule work as written. This is not currently load-bearing: all nine resolved primitives resolve on their root identity string alone, so the effective rule against today's bytes is that the contract's own root identifier contains the primitive's word.
findings.why_it_matters: The shipped description of the rule is accurate - it says exactly '$id, or a root-level _id or _schema value' and 'properties, patternProperties keys' - so this is not the description-outruns-code class. It is a note that the class pass 4 closed for five key names is closed by enumeration rather than by construction, and that the next prose-shaped field nobody thought of is admitted by default. The example-data inconsistency is the one half worth naming as an inconsistency rather than a width: the module gives a reason for excluding example identifiers and does not apply it to example names.

A member whose verify gate is blind to its headline repair cannot be witnessed on a green verify, and a witness chain that overstates its own independence is the one thing a witness must not pass.
